TIME-SERIES FORECASTING IN SAFETY-CRITICAL ENVIRONMENTS:
AN EU-AI-ACT-COMPLIANT OPEN-SOURCE PACKAGE

ABSTRACT
With spotforecast2-safe we present an integrated Compliance-by-Design approach to Python-
based point forecasting of time series in safety-critical environments. A review of the relevant
open-source tooling shows that existing compliance solutions operate consistently outside of the li-
brary to be used — e.g. as scanners, templates, or runtime layers. spotforecast2-safe takes
the inverse approach and anchors the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act,
in German: KI-VO), of IEC 61508, of the ISA/IEC 62443 standards series, and of the Cyber Re-
silience Act within the library: in application-programming-interface contracts, persistence formats,
and continuous-integration gates. The approach is operationalised by four non-negotiable code-
development rules (zero dead code, deterministic processing, fail-safe handling, minimal dependen-
cies) together with the corresponding process rules (model card, executable docstrings, CI workflows,
Common-Platform-Enumeration (CPE) identifier, REUSE-conformant licensing, release pipeline).
Interactive visualisation, hyperparameter tuning and automated machine learning (AutoML), as well
as deep-learning and large-language-model backends are deliberately excluded, because each of these
components either enlarges the attack surface, introduces non-determinism, or impairs reproducibil-
ity. A bidirectional traceability matrix maps every regulatory provision onto the corresponding
mechanism in the code; an end-to-end example of European-market electricity generation, trans-
mission, and consumption forecasting demonstrates the application. The package is open-source and
available under Affero General Public License (AGPL) 3.0-or-later.

Introduction
The practice of software development in the field of artificial intelligence (AI1) and in the field of critical infrastruc-
ture2 has, until now, evolved largely in separate software ecosystems. AI-based software development for time-series
forecasting favours feature-rich libraries that bundle visualisation, hyperparameter search, probabilistic deep-learning
backends, and interactive dashboards into a single installable package. Such broad libraries are excellently suited
to exploratory work and innovative research. However, this richness turns into a liability the moment the resulting
forecasting model is deployed in an environment that must withstand audits for safety-critical systems. Visualisation
tools, for instance, require the inclusion of a larger number of additional graphics libraries. The same holds for the
hyperparameter-tuning layer and for deep-learning models, which additionally exhibit very short release cycles, so that
the long-term reproducibility that regulators demand is not easily ensured.
A concrete review of the 2026 Python forecasting landscape confirms this tension. The three dominant Python libraries,
sktime (Löning, A. Bagnall, et al., 2019), Darts (Herzen et al., 2022), and skforecast (Amat Rodrigo and Escobar
Ortiz, 2025), ship extensive functionality that goes far beyond forecasting per se. The classical libraries (statsmodels,
pmdarima) are leaner but offer neither dedicated fail-safe semantics for invalid input nor a fixed CPE identifier for
vulnerability tracking.
When such software libraries are deployed in safety-critical environments, the regulatory requirements that arise —
among others — from Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on artificial intelligence (referred to below as the “EU AI Act” or, in
German, KI-VO) must be taken into account. The EU AI Act follows a risk-based approach: the regulatory intervention
is tailored to the concrete risk level, not to the technology as such (Stettinger, Weissensteiner, and Khastgir, 2024).
Figure 1 arranges the four resulting tiers (unacceptable, high, limited, and low or minimal risk) in their canonical
depiction as a pyramid of risk.

• Unacceptable risk. The EU AI Act prohibits manipulative AI systems using subliminal techniques, the targeted
exploitation of vulnerable groups, social scoring by public authorities, as well as real-time remote biometric
identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (subject to narrow exceptions).
• High risk. This category covers AI systems acting as a safety component of, or being themselves, a product
regulated by existing EU product-safety legislation (toys, aviation, motor vehicles, medical devices, lifts),
as well as systems deployed in the use cases listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act. Providers must conduct
an ex-ante conformity assessment, register the system in an EU database, and implement seven substantive
requirements: EU-1. human oversight, EU-2. technical robustness and safety, EU-3. privacy and data gover-
nance, EU-4. transparency, EU-5. diversity, non-discrimination and fairness, EU-6. social and environmental
well-being, and EU-7. accountability. These seven requirements derive from the Ethics Guidelines for Trust-
worthy AI of the High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence (AI-HLEG) (High-Level Expert Group
on Artificial Intelligence, 2019) and are operationalised by the Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI)
(High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2020; Stettinger, Weissensteiner, and Khastgir, 2024).
• Limited risk. For chatbots, emotion-recognition systems, biometric categorisation, and for systems that gener-
ate or manipulate image, audio, or video content (so-called deepfakes), transparency obligations apply: users
must be able to recognise that they are interacting with an AI system.
• Low or minimal risk. No additional obligations; the EU AI Act encourages voluntary codes of conduct under
which providers of non-high-risk systems may adopt the requirements imposed on high-risk systems.

The open-source software library spotforecast2-safe presented in this report is designed as a component for high-
risk forecasting applications, e.g. for load forecasting in grid operations. Table 1 shows the semantic mapping of the EU
AI Act articles to the seven high-risk requirements (EU-1 to EU-7). The EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council,
2024b) obliges providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to demonstrate compliance with all seven high-risk
requirements. When AI-research-grade software packages are used, a deployer3 inherits none of these demonstrations
from the software library itself. Such demonstrations may have to be re-established at considerable expense.
By contrast, spotforecast2-safe shifts this evidence-bearing inside the software library, so that the deployer in-
herits it. To this end, the design principles described in Chapter 4 are introduced. These principles require a specific
engineering decision and an accompanying test. The discipline of translating regulatory provisions into implementable,
verifiable software requirements while maintaining a bidirectional traceability between every provision and the mech-
anism that fulfills it is known as Legal-Requirements-Engineering (LRE) (Otto and Anton, 2007; Breaux and Antón,
2008). Kosenkov et al. (2024) provides a systematic survey of the field. LRE ensures that all relevant statutes, direc-
tives, recitals, explanatory background, and standards are integrated into the software development process to deliver
sustained legal compliance (Hense and Mustać, 2024). LRE means that legal requirements should be considered from
the very design stage of an AI system. This avoids tedious and potentially expensive adjustments at later stages of

development (compliance-by-design). Chapter 6.3 shows how the spotforecast2-safe software applies the LRE
discipline.
While compliance-monitoring libraries such as Deepchecks (Chorev et al., 2022) and Evidently AI4 partially cover
the evaluation side of the robustness requirement under Art. 15 EU AI Act,5 they sit on top of an already finished fore-
casting software and alter neither the provenance trail, nor determinism, nor the dependency footprint of the software
itself. Chapter B.1 and Chapter B.2 (in the appendix) show how the spotforecast2-safe software presented here
can be combined with the compliance-monitoring features of Deepchecks and Evidently AI.
A software library that rests on a software stack with dozens of unpinned dependencies is not unconditionally uncer-
tifiable; the cost of constructing the required evidence trail, however, grows with every additional dependency. The
pre-existing standards on functional safety6 make the same connection visible from the opposite direction: software
whose behaviour depends on uncontrolled external factors cannot be classified above Safety Integrity Level (SIL) 1
(International Electrotechnical Commission, 2010b) or Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL) A (International Or-
ganization for Standardization, 2018a) without a disproportionately large verification effort.
Cyber Resilience Act. The requirements EU-1 to EU-7 defined by the EU AI Act are, however, not the only regulatory
metrics that a forecasting library has to satisfy in order to be deployable in safety-critical environments. In indus-
trial deployment contexts, a forecasting library runs as a software component on level 2 or 3 of the Purdue reference
model7 (ISA-95 / IEC 62264), where the dominant cybersecurity framework is the ISA/IEC 62443 standards series
(IEC, 2009).8 Within the European Union (EU), the 62443 series — and EN IEC 62443-4-1 in particular — has, by
Commission Implementing Decision C(2025) 618 of 3 February 2025 (European Commission, 2025), been formally
designated as a reference standard within the framework of the standardisation request M/606 for harmonisation under
the now-in-force Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) (European Parliament and Council, 2024c); it furthermore shapes the
risk-management duties under Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS-2 Directive) (European Parliament and Council, 2022a)
as well as the Critical Entities Resilience Directive (CER Directive) (European Parliament and Council, 2022b). Fluchs
(2024) characterises 62443-2-1 as the “equivalent of ISO/IEC 27001 for cyber-physical systems (CPS)”. The part of
the standards series directly binding for spotforecast2-safe, however, is 62443-4-1 (see also Chapter 5.7.2).
Civil-law product liability. Beyond the public-law conformity and cybersecurity frameworks, the new Product Liability
Directive (PLD; Directive (EU) 2024/2853) (European Parliament and Council, 2024a) extends strict product liability
to software and AI systems: these are, for the first time, explicitly captured as a “product” within the meaning of
liability law, including integrated digital services and security-relevant post-market updates. The directive replaces the
1985 Product Liability Directive 85/374/EEC and applies to products placed on the market or put into service after
9 December 2026; by that date the Member States must also have completed national transposition. In Germany, the
directive is being implemented by the draft act on the modernisation of product-liability law (Deutscher Bundestag,
2026), which at the time of this report is undergoing parliamentary procedure (Bundestag printed paper 21/4297, first
reading on 4 March 2026). Open-source software developed or made available outside of a commercial activity remains
exempt from product liability. For a library released under AGPL-3.0-or-later such as spotforecast2-safe, liability
arises only where it is made available on the Union market in the course of a commercial activity — but there it carries
the same duties of care and documentation that the CRA and the EU AI Act impose.
Open-source carve-outs. There is an almost unsurveyable thicket of regulations that providers and deployers of AI
models or systems may have to take into account. The most prominent are Art. 50 and 51 of the EU AI Act, the EU
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Data Act, and the violation of copyright, personality, or labour rights.
This contribution deliberately confines itself, as a first foray of free and open-source software (FOSS) into KRITIS, to
the regulations mentioned at the outset.
• EU AI Act: open-source special rules.
On top of the FOSS exemption of the PLD, the EU AI Act
and the CRA each contain their own, mutually independent special rules for FOSS that are relevant for
spotforecast2-safe as a library released under AGPL-3.0-or-later. Art. 2(12) of the EU AI Act (Eu-
ropean Parliament and Council, 2024b) excludes AI systems released under a free or open-source licence in
principle from the regulation’s scope, but lifts that exception again for high-risk AI systems within the mean-
ing of Annex III, for prohibited practices under Art. 5 of the EU AI Act, and for transparency-bound systems

• CRA: open-source special rules. The CRA (European Parliament and Council, 2024c) complements this
scheme via Art. 24 CRA, which provides for reduced obligations for “open-source software stewards” —
typically not-for-profit or community-economic organisations that maintain FOSS projects on a long-term
basis — relative to the manufacturer duties of Art. 13 ff. CRA (a documented cybersecurity policy, coordinated
vulnerability handling, cooperation with market surveillance) and excludes the imposition of administrative
fines except for reporting duties. Recital 18 CRA further clarifies that the mere financial support of a FOSS
project does not preclude its classification as non-monetised.
• NIS-2: open-source special rules. NIS-2 (European Parliament and Council, 2022a) provides no explicit
FOSS exemption; its supply-chain duty under Art. 21(2)(d) NIS-2 binds the regulated KRITIS operator and
not the open-source maintainer, but propagates de facto into the FOSS ecosystem through contractual require-
ments. The relevant legal literature systematically analyses this entanglement (Colonna, 2025; van ’t Schip,
2025; Kikelj and Sabic, 2024).
Trustworthiness. A parallel research line addresses how the trustworthiness of a high-risk AI system is to be assessed.
Stettinger, Weissensteiner, and Khastgir (2024) propose a trustworthiness-assurance framework that decomposes the
EU AI Act requirements through a six-step iterative process into verifiable properties and connects AI-system engineer-
ing with the assurance argumentation of functional safety. The present report is compatible with this framework: every
process rule in Chapter 4 is an argumentation step, and the Mechanism column of Table 10 provides the substantiation.
Artificial intelligence and fundamental rights. The legal-scholarship background is set out by Raue et al. (2025), who
examines the interplay between the EU AI Act and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, anti-
discrimination law, and data protection law. Raue et al. (2025) is the authoritative reference when a deployer has to
translate the technical evidence documented here into a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under Art. 27
of the EU AI Act.

The spotforecast2-safe package attempts to bridge these gaps between software development in AI research and in
safety-critical applications. The starting point for the development of spotforecast2-safe is skforecast (Amat
Rodrigo and Escobar Ortiz, 2025). About one third of the safety-critical lines of code are a direct port from the
skforecast source code. Additional code implements the four code-development rules described in Chapter 4.1 (“no
dead code”, “deterministic transformations”, “fail-safe handling”, and “minimal scope”), as well as the four process
rules described in Chapter 4.2. Because of these rules, the feature scope of the software is reduced. To compensate
for this deliberate reduction, spotforecast2-safe is published as a subset of the broader open-source sister package
spotforecast2 (Bartz-Beielstein, 2026). The spotforecast2 package adds further features: interactive visualisa-
tion based on plotly and matplotlib, hyperparameter tuning via optuna and spotoptim, and model-explanation
tooling based on shap.
The remainder of this report describes the subset implemented by spotforecast2-safe. The report pursues three
objectives. First, it situates the package within the landscape of Python time-series tools and explains which features
have been deliberately omitted from the safety-critical subset and why (Chapter 2). Second, it documents the archi-
tecture (Chapter 3.1), the formal preprocessing and forecasting algorithms (Chapter 3.2 through Chapter 3.4), and the
safety-relevant design decisions shipped in the most recent versions (Chapter 4 through Chapter 5). Third, it maps the

2
Software packages for time-series forecasting
The Python time-series-forecasting ecosystem has grown strongly over the past decade and has also adopted implemen-
tations from the statistical programming language R (R Core Team, 2021). Foundational is the statsmodels package,
which provides ARIMA, SARIMAX, and exponential-smoothing models in line with the classical exposition by Box
et al. (2015). scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) deliberately abstains from time-series-specific functionality and
delegates such features to downstream libraries. The most relevant of these libraries are introduced briefly below.
skforecast (Amat Rodrigo and Escobar Ortiz, 2025) provides a Forecaster abstraction that wraps any scikit-
learn-compatible regressor into a recursive, direct, or multi-series forecaster. It is the closest conceptual relative of
the package documented here. From it we adopt the architecture of recursive forecasting, the rolling-origin split-
ter, and substantial parts of the modules _binner, _differentiator, and the residuals infrastructure. We do not
adopt the visualisation subsystem (which depends on matplotlib and plotly) or the hyperparameter tuning via
bayesian_search_forecaster (which relies on optuna and produces non-deterministic optimisation traces). These
tools are contained in the spotforecast2 package.
The unified Forecaster/BaseEstimator API of sktime (Löning, A. Bagnall, et al., 2019; Löning, T. Bagnall, et al.,
2020), which provides a wide range of models and validation schemes, is the most extensive of the libraries considered
here. However, the API is not fully compatible with that of scikit-learn, so that integrating regressors from that
ecosystem is not straightforward. Moreover, many models in sktime rely on statsmodels implementations that are
not optimised for the requirements of functional safety (e.g. no fail-safe handling of invalid inputs). Visualisation tools
and probabilistic backends are likewise absent.
The Nixtla ecosystem, which targets improvements in runtime throughput, implements three complementary libraries:
statsforecast (Garza, Challu, and Mergenthaler-Canseco, 2022) provides vectorised implementations of classical
models, trading model flexibility for aggressive runtime optimisation via Numba (Lam, Pitrou, and Seibert, 2015).
mlforecast extends the same API to gradient-boosting methods. neuralforecast offers deep-learning architectures
through a unified interface. The deep-learning backend immediately violates the rule of minimal scope.
Darts (Herzen et al., 2022) introduces a unified API for various time-series models. Its installation footprint is domi-
nated by optional dependencies whose behaviour influences the availability of model classes at import time. The same
applies to tsai, Merlion, and Kats (Oguiza, 2023; Bhatnagar et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022).
None of the libraries listed is deficient from an engineering standpoint. On the contrary, they constitute outstanding
research-grade software. However, software optimised for rapid exploration cannot automatically meet a SIL-3 software
verification budget without substantial deployer-specific rework. spotforecast2-safe shifts that rework into the
package itself, so that the deployer inherits the demonstrations rather than having to reproduce them.
3
The spotforecast2-safe package
3.1
Architecture
The spotforecast2-safe package is organised into three layers.
The lowest layer (forecaster/,
preprocessing/, model_selection/, data/) contains the estimator wrappers, transformers, and splitters that de-
rive most directly from skforecast. A middle layer (manager/) bundles an estimator together with an ExogBuilder,
a configurator, a logger, and a persistence layer into a deployable unit. The top layer (processing/ and tasks/) pro-
vides end-to-end pipelines that compose the two lower layers into console scripts.

3.2
Preprocessing
The preprocessing sub-package contains four kinds of transformer: cyclical encoders that map periodic calendar fea-
tures (hour of day, day of week, day of year) into a smooth representation; interpolators that reconstruct short gaps under
an explicit contract; a quantile binner that discretises a continuous feature into equal-frequency bins; and a differentia-
tor that applies a finite-difference operator. All four transformers inherit from sklearn.base.TransformerMixin
and are therefore composable within an sklearn Pipeline.
3.3
Forecasting
The forecasting layer implements the recursive multi-step strategy: a single scalar one-step-ahead model is trained
and then iterated to produce horizons of arbitrary length (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, 2021). For 𝑦𝑡, lags ℒ=
{ℓ1, … , ℓ𝑝}, window features 𝑤𝑡(e.g. moving averages), and an exogenous vector 𝑥𝑡, the forecaster learns
̂𝑦𝑡= 𝑓(𝑦𝑡−ℓ1, … , 𝑦𝑡−ℓ𝑝, 𝑤𝑡, 𝑥𝑡) ,
and the ℎ-step forecast is obtained recursively:
̂𝑦𝑡+ℎ= 𝑓( ̃𝑦𝑡+ℎ−ℓ1, … , ̃𝑦𝑡+ℎ−ℓ𝑝, 𝑤𝑡+ℎ, 𝑥𝑡+ℎ) ,
where ̃𝑦𝑠= 𝑦𝑠for 𝑠≤𝑡and ̃𝑦𝑠= ̂𝑦𝑠otherwise.
The advantage of recursive strategies in a safety-critical context is that the training and evaluation paths are coupled
by construction: the same feature-matrix builder produces both the training features and the features used at prediction
time, so that feature-skew errors become a build-time rather than a run-time error class. In addition, a separate model
can be trained for each individual prediction quantity to achieve better accuracy, at the cost of an ℎ-fold number of
models.
Prediction intervals are computed by bootstrap-resampling the in-sample residuals. For a desired coverage 1 −𝛼, the
residuals 𝜀1, … , 𝜀𝑁are drawn with replacement and added to the recursive point forecast; this yields an empirical
interval between the 𝛼/2 and 1 −𝛼/2 quantiles. This is the same procedure as in skforecast; given a seed, it is
deterministic and does not require a probabilistic regressor.
The backend regressors shipped with the package are LightGBM (Ke et al., 2017) and XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin,
2016), implemented as ForecasterRecursiveLGBM and ForecasterRecursiveXGB respectively. Both are strong

The “M-

3.4
Testing
A naive application of sklearn.model_selection.KFold to a time-indexed series leaks the future into the training
set. Time-series-aware splitters remedy this by forcing the training segment to precede the test segment in time. The
package provides two such splitters as well as a backtesting driver.
TimeSeriesFold realises the growing-window protocol. Let 𝑇0 be initial_train_size, 𝑠be steps, and ℎthe
forecast horizon. The splitter yields train/test index pairs of the form ([0, 𝑇0 + 𝑘⋅𝑠), [𝑇0 + 𝑘⋅𝑠, 𝑇0 + 𝑘⋅𝑠+ ℎ))
for 𝑘= 0, 1, 2, …. A refit flag determines whether the forecaster is re-trained at each fold or fitted only once at
the beginning. For scenarios in which even the refit cost is prohibitive, the parameter fold_stride permits non-
overlapping folds that nevertheless cover a large test region; refit work is thus amortised across multiple test regions.

because OpenMP scheduling is a known source of cross-platform non-determinism.
Bergmeir and Benitez (2012) provides the theoretical justification: under standard stationarity assumptions, the
forward-chaining cross-validation estimator of the mean-squared one-step-ahead prediction error is consistent, whereas
the ordinary 𝑘-fold cross-validation estimator is not. The package therefore exposes exclusively the two time-aware
splitters; from the manager layer there is no escape route to the sklearn originals.
4
Design principles
The design principles fall into two parallel categories. The code-development rules restrict which constituents the
source code may contain; they are enforced at commit time by a test or by a linter9. The process rules restrict how
the package is developed, shipped, and operated, and are met by MODEL_CARD.md, CI workflows, and the release
pipeline rather than by source-code tests. Both categories are required: the code-development rules alone do not
suﬀice to discharge the regulatory duties of traceability, threat modelling, data governance, supply-chain integrity, and
operational observability.
4.1
Code-development rules
The four non-negotiable code rules are:
• CR-1. No dead code. “Dead code” is code whose removal does not affect the program’s behaviour. No
function, class, or branch ships without a test or an executable docstring example reaching it. A test suite
test_docstring_examples_*.py enforces this.
• CR-2. Deterministic transformations. Same input, same bit-level output. Random-number generators are
seeded; dictionary iteration order is not relied upon; joblib parallelism is pinned to a fixed n_jobs argument.
No generation of random numbers without a seed and no dependence on Python dictionary iteration orders.
• CR-3. Fail-safe handling. Invalid inputs raise an explicit exception rather than being silently imputed or co-
erced. For example, NaN values, wrong dtypes, or missing indices raise explicit ValueError or TypeError
exceptions.
Silent imputation is available only behind a typed Literal["raise", "ffill_bfill",
"passthrough"] switch that must be set explicitly.

5.1.1
Fail-safe NaN handling
Every tabular measurement may be missing — because a weather station reports no data for an hour, because a power
meter has been restarted, or because an import error left a cell empty. In Python such a gap is marked by the special
12


SPOTFORECAST2-SAFE - APRIL 28, 2026
value NaN (“Not a Number”), analogous to a blank field on a questionnaire that has not yet been answered. What matters
for downstream processing is how the next-stage software reacts to such a field: should it estimate the empty value and
continue, or should it halt and demand a decision from the deployer?
The Python time-series libraries established in this space mostly follow the pattern of “silently keep going”. pandas
(McKinney, 2010) interpolates missing values linearly between neighbours via Series.interpolate() and leaves
leading and trailing gaps untouched, without warning the caller; scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) replaces NaN
by the column mean by default through the SimpleImputer; the forecasting package skforecast (Amat Rodrigo and
Escobar Ortiz, 2025) that builds on top of it propagates remaining NaN through to the forecast, where they mix with
the regular model error; Darts (Herzen et al., 2022) and statsmodels follow the same line. For exploratory work this
stance is convenient — it permits rapid prototyping with messy data. For deployment in safety-critical environments,
however, e.g. electric load forecasting for a grid operator, it is exactly the case that Art. 15 of the EU AI Act, IEC
61508, and ISO 26262 seek to avoid: an operator may dispatch on the basis of an apparently complete forecast without
noticing that part of the input data was missing and was substituted by the package without enquiry.
A concrete example makes the difference clear: suppose a grid dispatcher is to forecast hourly load for the coming
day, and the weather API returns no temperature value for a single hour — say 03:00. Under the silent approach,
the forecasting package would interpolate the value linearly between 02:00 and 04:00, return the load forecast with
an apparently normal confidence interval, and the dispatcher would schedule the 03:00 hour as usual. The gap in the
measurements would be visible only in the preprocessing log — and only if someone takes the trouble to read it. Under
the fail-safe approach, by contrast, the transformer aborts with an explicit error message, the continuous-integration
pipeline raises an alarm, and the deployer must take a documented decision: switch to a fallback model, flag the 03:00
hour as invalid, or close the gap deliberately and record that decision in the audit log.
spotforecast2-safe inverts the default of the libraries listed above. The transformer LinearlyInterpolateTS
accepts a keyword on_missing that takes only three values, and the default is "raise":
from spotforecast2_safe.preprocessing import LinearlyInterpolateTS
# Raises ValueError if NaN values remain after interpolation:
t = LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="raise")
# Explicit opt-in to forward/backward fill of the endpoints:
t = LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="ffill_bfill")
# The caller commits to handling NaN downstream:
t = LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="passthrough")
The abort under "raise" is the desired outcome, not a fault: the error becomes visible, reaches the CI pipeline, and
forces the deployer to take an explicit decision. The central point is that the deployer cannot, in an audit, claim to have
overlooked the data gap — because the package actively reported it. The mechanism therefore addresses Art. 15 of the
EU AI Act (accuracy and robustness) (European Parliament and Council, 2024b), the fail-safe principle of IEC 61508-
3 (International Electrotechnical Commission, 2010a), and ISO 26262-6 §8.4.5 (prohibition of silent zero-defaults)
(International Organization for Standardization, 2018b) directly.
An executable docstring test enforces that every Literal value produces the documented behaviour.

version of a product is affected as soon as a CVE is reported under the same CPE — in particular through the catalogue
of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency
(CISA) (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, 2023). Without a fixed CPE, scanners would have to map
the package name to a CPE value via local heuristics; that works for unambiguously named packages but yields false
positives in the case of name collisions or renamings, or leaves real vulnerabilities undetected.
The distinguishing feature of spotforecast2-safe is that the CPE identifier is not guessed by downstream tools but
is fixed within the package itself. Most Python packages declare no CPE and rely on the heuristics of scanners such as
pip-audit or safety. By contrast, the file src/spotforecast2_safe/utils/cpe.py contains the canonical CPE
string, and tests/test_cpe.py verifies it in a round-trip (serialisation →deserialisation →identical object). This el-
evates the identifier to a first-class API contract: a breaking change — e.g. a switch of the vendor string or product name
— requires a Conventional-Commits subject feat!:, which forces a major version bump via semantic-release and
appears as an entry in the CHANGELOG.md. A deployer can therefore rely on the CPE listed in their SBOM remaining
stable across the entire minor-version line.
From a regulatory perspective, this approach matches the three duties that the fixed CPE directly serves: Annex I Part II
No. 1 CRA (European Parliament and Council, 2024c) requires the manufacturer of a product with digital elements
to produce a software bill of materials; Art. 72 of the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) obliges
providers of high-risk AI systems to perform post-market monitoring, which presupposes a reliable attribution of CVE
reports to the own product; and the process area SM (Security Management) of IEC 62443-4-1 (IEC, 2018) requires
an inventory of third-party components, which in this mechanism is the SBOM. The concrete benefit: a deployer no
longer has to rely on a scanner’s guess as to which of their installed packages a particular CVE applies to, but can derive
the affectedness deterministically from the CPE fixed in the package.
5.7
ISA/IEC 62443 and the CPS security context
5.7.1
The 62443 standards series in overview
The ISA/IEC 62443 standards family is organised into four groups:
1. General (Part 1 — terminology and models (IEC, 2009)),
2. Policies and procedures (Part 2 — programmes for asset owners (IEC, 2024) and service providers (IEC,
2023)),
3. System (Part 3 — risk assessment (IEC, 2020) and security requirements at the system level (IEC, 2013)), and
4. Component (Part 4 — secure product development (IEC, 2018) and technical requirements for components
(IEC, 2019)).
In the taxonomy of 62443-4-2, a time-series forecasting library is a Software Application (alongside Embedded Device,
Host Device, and Network Device); it therefore inherits the Software-Application-Requirements (SAR) subset of the
component catalogue rather than the full Embedded Device profile. Table 4 summarises this organisation.
NIST SP 800-82r3 (Stouffer et al., 2023) presents the Purdue model, the ISA/IEC 62443 view, and the Industrial-
Internet-Consortium (IIC) tier model side by side as three alternative segmentation frameworks; Figure 3 reproduces
this juxtaposition. The 62443 view there uses zones and conduits (Enterprise →Conduit →DMZ →Control Center →
Conduit →Basic Process Control System (BPCS) →Conduit →Safety Instrumented System (SIS)) instead of Purdue
levels 0–5. The 62443 series therefore does not map 1:1 onto Purdue levels, because its parts are organised by role
— asset owner, service provider, system integrator, component manufacturer — not by network levels. Industrial
practice nevertheless commonly uses a mapping to the Purdue level that follows the scope of the 62443 parts, because
it eases reviewers’ and auditors’ mental bridge between network segmentation and standardised requirements. Table 5
summarises this heuristic mapping; 62443-1-1 (IEC, 2009) (terminology and models) applies cross-cuttingly at all
levels.

5.7.2
Secure product-development lifecycle (62443-4-1)
IEC 62443-4-1 builds on Microsoft’s Security Development Lifecycle (SDL) (Howard and Lipner, 2006). SDL de-
scribes a process in which every development phase (requirements, design, implementation, verification, release, re-
sponse) is paired with an explicit security activity such as threat modelling, static analysis, fuzz testing, and incident
response. SDL defines eight process areas on four maturity levels. Table 6 reports the current evidence status for each
practice in spotforecast2-safe. The package reaches ML 2 Managed across all eight practices; ML 3 Defined
requires a formal threat model and a documented security-assessment report, which are tracked in the M1–M7 backlog
of REVIEW_FINDINGS.md.
5.7.3
Foundational requirements and security levels (62443-3-3 and 62443-4-2)
IEC 62443-3-3 and 62443-4-2 share seven foundational requirements (Foundational Requirements: FR 1 identification
and authentication control, FR 2 use control, FR 3 system integrity, FR 4 data confidentiality, FR 5 restricted data
flow, FR 6 timely response to events, FR 7 resource availability) and four security levels (Security Level: SL 1 protec-
tion against casual or coincidental violation up to SL 4 protection against intentional attacks by actors with extended
resources).
A pure software library cannot, on its own, satisfy requirements that depend on the surrounding system (network
segmentation (FR 5) and authentication (FR 1) are the clearest examples), but it can avoid breaking those requirements,
and that is exactly the stance that spotforecast2-safe adopts. FR 3 (system integrity) is supported by deterministic
transformations, pinned dependencies, and SPDX-tracked provenance; FR 6 (timely response to events) is supported by
tight exception handling and structured logging (Chapter 5); FR 7 (resource availability) is supported by the minimal-
scope rule, which caps the transitive dependency closure. The library therefore supports an SL 2 system when it is
itself embedded into an SL 2 zone; the security level is a property of the zone, not of the library in isolation.
5.7.4
CPS specifics that shape the software design
Fluchs and Rudolph (2019) and Fluchs (2024) highlight four specifics of CPS cybersecurity that distinguish it from
classical IT security and that shape the design of the present package:
1. Long lifecycles. Industrial plants are operated for 20 to 40 years; a forecasting model shipped today may still
be producing setpoints in 2050. Deterministic serialisation, a pinned public API, and a CPE identifier are
necessary preconditions for retrospective verifiability across that horizon.
2. Convergence of safety and security. A forecast that drives a physical actuator is a safety-functional input. The
technical report IEC TR 63069 explicitly addresses the joint safety-and-security problem; the package adopts
its conclusion that safety decisions, once taken, must not be overwritten by a later security fix — hence the
fail-safe default “exception on invalid input” rather than a silent data correction.
3. Late security integration as a dominant root cause of failure. Interviews with engineers from INEOS and
HIMA reported by Fluchs (2024) show that security is typically appended after the basic-engineering phase,
i.e. once the design-time-favourable decisions (network topology, component selection) have already been

6.1
EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 25059
The code and process rules of Chapter 4 map onto individual provisions of the EU AI Act, IEC 61508-3, ISO 26262-6,
the ISA/IEC 62443 standards series, and the CRA.
6.1.1
Article 4 of the EU AI Act (AI literacy)
Article 4 of the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) obliges providers and deployers to ensure that
their staff and other persons operating or using an AI system on their behalf possess a suﬀicient level of AI literacy,
calibrated to the use context and to the groups of persons on which the system acts. spotforecast2-safe is designed
so that a process engineer without formal training in machine learning can attain that threshold by reading the package
alone. Three mechanisms contribute. First, every public transformer and every forecaster carries executable docstring
examples, so that the intended behaviour can be learnt by running small, self-contained snippets and is not dependent
on the study of external manuals. Second, typed contracts make the pre- and post-conditions of every call visible at

the call site; this lowers the expert knowledge required to read a training script correctly. Third, the structured audit
log (rule 4 in Chapter 4) discloses, line by line, the sequence of decisions taken by a running forecaster, so that the
deployer’s staff can review the operational behaviour after the fact. The model-related MODEL_CARD.md complements
these mechanisms by recording the intended deployment frame and the known limits in a language with which non-
specialist operating personnel can also work. Taken together, these design choices lower the AI-literacy threshold the
deployer must reach in order to supervise the system responsibly, and thereby support the obligation of Art. 4 of the
EU AI Act directly.
6.1.2
Article 9 of the EU AI Act (risk management)
Article 9 of the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) obliges the provider of a high-risk AI system to
establish, implement, document, and maintain a risk-management system (Risk Management System, RMS) (paragraph
1). This is to be understood as a continuous, iterative process across the entire lifecycle and comprises four steps
(paragraph 2): identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks (Art. 9(2)(a) of the EU AI Act);
estimation and evaluation of risks in the intended use and under reasonably foreseeable misuse (Art. 9(2)(b) of the EU
AI Act); evaluation of further risks from the post-market monitoring system under Art. 72 of the EU AI Act (Art. 9(2)(c)
of the EU AI Act); and the adoption of suitable, targeted risk-management measures (Art. 9(2)(d) of the EU AI Act).
The measures must take into account the combined interplay of the requirements of Chapter III Section 2 (paragraph
4) and must be such that the residual risks remaining are acceptable (paragraph 5). The system must be tested against
pre-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds (paragraphs 6 and 8), in particular with regard to minors and other
vulnerable groups (paragraph 9); under parallel regulation it may be combined with existing Union risk-management
processes (paragraph 10).
For a forecasting library embedded as a component, the same shared responsibility described in Chapter 6.1.3 and
Chapter 6.1.12 recurs: the provider of the embedded high-risk system remains the primary addressee of the RMS
duty. spotforecast2-safe, however, covers the two provider-side duties that a library can address on its own: the
risk-mitigating design of its own code (Art. 9(3) and Art. 9(5)(a) of the EU AI Act) and the supply of the technical
information on which the provider builds its own RMS (Art. 9(5)(c) of the EU AI Act). Three mechanisms carry this
work.
1. Threat-model-based risk identification (Art. 9(2)(a) and (b) of the EU AI Act). For every network-facing
module (downloader/entsoe.py, weather/weather_client.py) a STRIDE table is maintained in
CONTRIBUTING.md; every change of the attack surface requires, via the pull-request template, an updated
threat entry in the same commit. This represents the identification and evaluation steps for the intended use
and reasonably foreseeable misuse of the network-mediated part of the library. For the data-side part, the
typed on_missing contract (see Chapter 6.1.3) acts as misuse early-warning: a missing or non-numerical
input is not silently imputed but raised to a documentation-required exception.
2. Design-side risk mitigation (Art. 9(2)(d) and Art. 9(5)(a) and (b) of the EU AI Act). The four code rules
of Chapter 4 (CR-1 No dead code, CR-2 Determinism, CR-3 Fail-safe, CR-4 Minimal CVE attack surface)
and the four process rules (PR-1 Traceability, PR-2 Threat model, PR-3 Signed supply chain, PR-4 Structured
audit log) are the concrete risk-management measures anchored in source code and the development pipeline.
They eliminate certain classes of risk through the design of the library (Art. 9(5)(a) of the EU AI Act) rather
than through downstream usage notices, and are, in the sense of Art. 9(4) of the EU AI Act, explicitly aligned
with the interplay of the remaining requirements of Chapter III Section 2: the mapping is laid out row by row
in Table 10 and summarised visually in Figure 5.
3. Continuous testing and feedback from monitoring (Art. 9(2)(c) and Art. 9(6) and (8) of the EU AI Act). The log
instrumentation described in Chapter 6.1.12 feeds events observed after placing on the market back into risk
analysis; the executable docstrings run via tests/test_docstring_examples_*.py, the minimum thresh-
old of 80 % line coverage fixed in pyproject.toml and the rolling-origin cross-validation split_ts_cv
together form the test layer required by Art. 9(6) and (8) against pre-defined metrics. CodeQL, Scorecard, and
Dependabot extend that test layer with security-oriented checks across the whole lifecycle.
Article 9(9) of the EU AI Act (adverse impact on minors and other vulnerable groups) does not directly apply to
the typical use case of electric load forecasting, because the forecast result does not carry decisions about individual

Article 10 of the EU AI Act (data governance)
Article 10 of the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) obliges the provider of a high-risk AI system
to data-governance measures across training, validation, and test datasets (paragraphs 1–4) and contains an exception
rule for special categories of personal data (paragraph 5) together with a scope limitation for pure inference systems
(paragraph 6). For a forecasting library that does not itself ship training data, this implies a shared responsibility: the
deployer remains the primary addressee of the substantive requirements; the package provides the technical infrastruc-
ture that allows the deployer to satisfy them and prevents them from being silently bypassed. Three mechanisms carry
this support.
1. Documented design choices and assumptions (Art. 10(2)(a) and (d) of the EU AI Act).
The structured
MODEL_CARD.md framework (see Chapter 6.1.4), with sections Uses, Bias, Risks, and Limitations, Evalua-
tion, and Environmental Impact, forces the deployer to record the relevant design choices and the assumptions
about the input data in writing.
2. Data provenance and preprocessing (Art. 10(2)(b) and (c) of the EU AI Act). Every Forecaster object
persists in its state the provenance of the data on which it was fitted — source URL, retrieval timestamp, and
content hash. For live-data paths, the adapters downloader/entsoe.py for ENTSO-E (ENTSO-E, 2024) and
weather/weather_client.py for Open-Meteo (Zippenfenig, 2024) are available; both record the retrieval
parameters in the persisted state. The only shipped preprocessing with data-changing semantics — linear
interpolation to fill missing timestamps — is encapsulated by the typed on_missing switch (see Chapter 4.1,
CR-3) so that it does not take effect silently but only after an explicit opt-in by the deployer. Annotation and
labelling do not arise in the regression-based forecasting use case.
3. Detection of data gaps (Art. 10(2)(h) of the EU AI Act). The fail-safe default on_missing="raise" turns
a silently-bypassed data gap into a discoverable, documentation- required event. The deployer is forced to
identify the gap as such and to take a documented decision (model fallback, marking as invalid, or explicit opt-
in to interpolation). This operationalises the “identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings” required
by Art. 10(2)(h) of the EU AI Act.
For the bias requirements (Art. 10(2)(f) and (g) of the EU AI Act) and the representativeness duty (Art. 10(3) of
the EU AI Act), assessment lies with the deployer, because biases arise only from the interplay of training data and
deployment scenario; the library supports verifiability through deterministic transformations (CR-2, see Chapter 6.1.8),
so that repeated experiments on the same dataset deliver bit-identical results and deviations can be attributed exclusively
to data differences. The representativeness can be checked empirically by the deployer with the ported rolling-origin
cross-validation split_ts_cv. Special categories of personal data (Art. 10(5) of the EU AI Act) do not arise in the
typical load-forecasting use case. If the package is used exclusively for inference with an already-trained model, the
scope of Art. 10(2) to (5) of the EU AI Act narrows under Art. 10(6) of the EU AI Act to the test dataset. This is a
configuration that the Forecaster persistence mechanism expressly supports through content hashes of the training
data.

6.1.8
Article 15 of the EU AI Act (accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity)
Article 15 of the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) describes accuracy, robustness, and cyberse-
curity for high-risk AI systems; paragraph 1 requires that these properties be delivered consistently “throughout their
lifecycle”, paragraph 4 demands resilience against errors, faults, and inconsistencies. On the implementation side of
spotforecast2-safe, this consistency requirement is met through a consistently deterministic execution path se-
cured on three layers. At the estimator level, LightGBM and XGBoost are always instantiated with a random_state
passed through by the wrapper; in addition, the options deterministic=True and force_col_wise=True are set
for LightGBM to remove the difference between row-wise and column-wise histogram construction on multi-core
systems. At the feature level, the order of concatenation of exogenous features is Python-version-stable, because the
ExogBuilder stores its components in a list rather than a dictionary. At the I/O level, a Parquet round-trip preserves
the dtypes but not the frequency of the DatetimeIndex; the cache reader therefore compares value-based, not frequency-
based, and the dedicated test suite tests/test_weather_client.py::TestWeatherServiceCache fixes this be-
haviour. The consistent performance across the lifecycle required by Art. 15(1) of the EU AI Act is thus evidenced in
a machine-verifiable, deployer-reproducible form.
In addition to robustness, the cybersecurity requirement under Art. 15(5) of the EU AI Act addresses the defence and
tracking of vulnerabilities. The CPE 2.3 identifier fixed in the package, described in detail in Chapter 5.6 (Cheikes,
Waltermire, and Scarfone, 2011), is the technical link that downstream vulnerability scanners use to assign a CVE
reported under the same CPE deterministically to the installed package version; without this fixing, scanners would
have to rely on heuristic package-name matches, with the well-known false-positive and miss risks.
Beyond the binding obligations of the regulation, the AI-specific extension of the Systems and software Quality Re-
quirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) standards series, ISO/IEC 25059:2023 (International Organization for Standard-
ization, 2023), provides the quality vocabulary that the expected harmonised CEN-CENELEC standards under Art. 40
of the EU AI Act are likely to adopt. Its quality model refines the sub-characteristics functional correctness, robust-
ness, and user controllability of ISO/IEC 25010 for AI systems and is therefore the natural technical counterpart to
Art. 15 of the EU AI Act. The 2023 edition is currently being revised: the Draft International Standard (DIS) ISO/IEC
25059:2025 is in the survey procedure, and an EU-AI-Act-aligned European edition (Preliminary European Norm,
prEN ISO/IEC 25059) is expected, via the Joint Technical Committee 21 (JTC 21) of CEN-CENELEC, for public
enquiry.

Article 17 of the EU AI Act (quality-management system)
The EU AI Act organises the provider-side duties around Art. 17 of the EU AI Act; this requires a documented quality-
management system (QMS) that integrates the individual substantive duties (risk management in Art. 9 of the EU AI
Act, data governance in Art. 10 of the EU AI Act, technical documentation in Art. 11 of the EU AI Act, record-keeping
in Art. 12 of the EU AI Act, transparency in Art. 13 of the EU AI Act, accuracy and robustness in Art. 15 of the EU AI
Act) with the provider-side process duties (record-keeping of the provider under Art. 18 of the EU AI Act, post-market
monitoring under Art. 72 of the EU AI Act, and reporting of serious incidents under Art. 73 of the EU AI Act). Table 10
therefore contains an “EU AI Act Art. 17 row” whose mechanism column points to the mechanisms used to satisfy the
respective sub-duty and cross-references the adjacent rows. A deployer preparing a conformity assessment can read
the “EU AI Act Art. 17 row” as an index into the rest of the table.
A mechanism not explicitly required by Art. 17 of the EU AI Act, but indispensable for a software provider’s QMS, is
licence traceability. spotforecast2-safe satisfies it through REUSE v3.0 conformance (detailed in Chapter 5.2.3):
every source file, every data fixture, and every test carries an SPDX header; uv run reuse lint is integrated into
pre-commit and is run on every commit; .reuse/dep5 resolves the licence of the few externally licensed files. From
this conformance, the deployer can at any time generate a SPDX-3.0-JSON document via reuse spdx and feed it into

Article 73 of the EU AI Act (reporting of serious incidents)
Article 73 of the EU AI Act (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) obliges the provider of a high-risk AI system

the latest 10 days in the case of death (paragraph 4). An initially incomplete first report may be supplemented by a
complete follow-up report (paragraph 5). After the report, the provider promptly conducts its own investigations (risk
assessment and corrective measures) and cooperates with the competent authorities; unilateral changes to the system
that could impair a subsequent root-cause analysis are prohibited (Art. 73(6) of the EU AI Act).
For a forecasting library embedded as a component into a high-risk AI system, a shared responsibility applies here too:
the provider of the embedded system, regularly the deployer-integrator that puts the library to use, remains the primary
addressee of the reporting duty. The package provides three mechanisms that enable the provider to meet the deadlines
of Art. 73 of the EU AI Act technically and to settle the investigation and correction chain required by Art. 73(6) of the
EU AI Act in a verifiable manner.
1. Confidential reporting channel and version policy. The file SECURITY.md in the repository establishes GitHub
Private Security Advisories as the primary channel for confidential reporting; as a fallback, the maintainers’
email address is available. Public issues are explicitly excluded. The published response commitments (ac-
knowledgement within 24 hours, initial assessment within 3 working days, coordinated public disclosure only
after a correction has been made available) are temporally compatible with the 2-day and 10-day deadlines
of Art. 73(3) and (4) of the EU AI Act. SECURITY.md additionally documents the window of supported ver-
sions (0.3.x with full support until October 2027, 0.2.x with limited support until February 2026), so that the
provider can clarify, before reporting, on which version the investigation will be based; the CODEOWNERS file
names the maintainers responsible for releases and makes the cooperation axis required by Art. 73(6) of the
EU AI Act traceable.
2. Early-warning signals. Three automated workflows supply providers and maintainers with early warnings
before an incident reaches market surveillance: the codeql.yml workflow for static security analysis, the
scorecard.yml workflow for the weekly OpenSSF Scorecard assessment of the supply chain (see Chap-
ter 6.1.8), and Dependabot for dependency and supply-chain alerts. In IEC 62443-4-1 terminology, these
workflows fill the process area DM (Defect Management); in EU AI Act terminology they create the knowl-
edge state on the basis of which the provider can date the start of the reporting deadlines at all.
3. Verifiable corrective measure.
After advisory triage, the Semantic-Release pipeline (see Chapter 6.1.6)
produces a new signed release with the corresponding correction. Delivery integrity is secured through
Sigstore-based keyless OIDC signatures and entry into the Rekor transparency log; the accompanying Cy-

Example: forecasting electric load
This section walks through the complete spotforecast2-safe pipeline on a synthetic load series that reproduces
the daily and weekly patterns of the ENTSO-E France time zone. Synthetic rather than live data are used so that
document generation remains deterministic and offline-capable; the module downloader/entsoe.py and an Open-
Meteo adapter (Zippenfenig, 2024) provide the corresponding live-data paths for production deployment.
The tutorial is deliberately written so that a reader with a legal background and no experience in statistics or time-series
analysis can follow every step. Each of the ten steps below consists of a short explanation of what happens and why,
together with a code block that is executed live when the report is rendered. We use exclusively the interface of the
spotforecast2-safe library; the actual estimator (LightGBM) and the cyclical feature encoding are encapsulated in
the wrapper classes, so that a user does not have to call them directly.

rule PR-4.

Step 6: instantiate and train the forecaster
The class ForecasterRecursiveLGBM encapsulates a LightGBM estimator with deterministic hyperparameters and
automatic lag management. Lags are the past values that the model uses as input — with lags=168 the model sees,
for every hour, the last full week as context, which is decisive for the weekly seasonality (weekday versus weekend).
“Recursive” means that the forecast for one hour serves in turn as input for the next hour when forecasting several
steps into the future. So that the model reliably learns the recurring daily and weekly patterns, we replace the default
LightGBM estimator with a richer variant with more trees, a lower learning rate, and a larger leaf count. With the call
to fit, the model performs one training round on the training data.

Discussion
This report constitutes a first approximation, with no claim to completeness, of the development of an EU-AI-Act-
compliant package for time-series point forecasting. The EU has declared the “digital decade”. The EU AI Act is only
one of several planned regulations and directives. As-yet-unknown future threat scenarios will lead the legislator to
develop further regulations protecting critical infrastructure (KRITIS), which may affect the development of AI appli-
cations. It is therefore to be expected that the requirements for the development of AI applications in the KRITIS sector
36


SPOTFORECAST2-SAFE - APRIL 28, 2026
will continue to grow over the coming years. By means of a consistently applied PDCA cycle, spotforecast2-safe
is continuously developed further in order to meet the evolving regulatory requirements and to establish the practice of
EU-AI-Act-compliant development in time-series forecasting.
The scope of the package described here is deliberately narrow. Three classes of functionality (interactive visualisation,
hyperparameter search, deep-learning backends) are explicitly out of scope and are not included. They are provided
by the sister package spotforecast2 (Bartz-Beielstein, 2026), which is not subject to the EU-AI-Act conformance
rules. The package spotforecast2_safe described here concentrates on delivering a robust, transparent, and verifi-
able core for time-series point forecasting that satisfies the requirements of the EU AI Act. To this end, LRE principles
are embedded into the library architecture in order to ensure traceability from regulatory requirements to code mecha-
nisms (compliance-by-design), to maintain the technical documentation, and to ensure compliance with record-keeping
obligations. A review of the literature and of the relevant repositories shows (as of April 2026) that the LRE disci-
pline has not previously been applied in the area of Python-based time-series forecasting: neither sktime (Löning, A.
Bagnall, et al., 2019), Darts (Herzen et al., 2022), skforecast (Amat Rodrigo and Escobar Ortiz, 2025), nor the clas-
sical libraries statsmodels and pmdarima carries bidirectional traceability between regulatory provisions and code
mechanisms, repository-checked conformity evidence, or contracts built into the code with respect to the EU AI Act,

exist that operationalise LRE-adjacent practice without referring to time-series forecasting: COMPL-AI (Guldimann
et al., 2024) (ETH Zürich, INSAIT, LatticeFlow AI; Apache 2.0) provides the first technical interpretation of the EU
AI Act and an open-source benchmarking suite for large language models; TechOps (Lucaj et al., 2025) provides open

A.2 Uses
A.2.1
Direct Use
• Safety-critical forecasting pipelines: Preparation of time series data for regression models in auditable
environments (energy supply, finance, industrial monitoring).
• Embedded / edge AI: Runs in resource-constrained environments where heavyweight ML frameworks
are not available.
• Reproducible research: Bit-level reproducible N-to-1 lag transformations, no hidden stochastics.
A.2.2
Downstream Use
• Feeding the generated feature matrices into scikit-learn regressors, lightgbm, or xgboost via the
bundled ForecasterRecursiveLGBM / ForecasterRecursiveXGB wrappers.
• Building custom recursive multi-step forecasters on top of the ForecasterRecursiveModel base class
in spotforecast2_safe.manager.models.
A.2.3
Out-of-Scope Use
• Interactive visualization: Deliberately no plotting code ships in this package; no Plotly, no Matplotlib.
• Automated hyperparameter tuning: Must run outside the safe environment (e.g., in a separate
spotforecast2 / spotoptim / Optuna workflow).
• Silent data cleaning: NaN / Inf values raise ValueError; the package does not silently impute.
A.3
A.3 Bias, Risks, and Limitations
• Downstream regressor drift: spotforecast2-safe performs deterministic feature engineering, not
forecasting by itself. Accuracy is bounded by the regressor and the training data; concept drift, season-
ality shifts, or regime changes in the downstream model will silently degrade forecasts.
• Lag-feature leakage when bypassing ExogBuilder: Users who construct lag or calendar features
outside the provided builders risk leaking target values into the feature row for timestamp t. The bundled
ExogBuilder / task_n_to_1 paths are leakage-free by construction; hand-rolled pipelines are not.
• Multi-threaded inference determinism: The bit-level reproducibility guarantee assumes single-
threaded execution or an explicitly pinned n_jobs=1 on the downstream regressor. Thread-pool sched-
ulers (e.g., LightGBM’s default n_jobs=-1) may reorder floating-point reductions.
• Memory for large series: Creating the lag matrix duplicates the input (𝑇× 𝑤). For 𝑇> 107 this can
exhaust memory; chunking is the caller’s responsibility.
• Living standards: IEC 61508 / ISO 26262 / EU AI Act references reflect the text as of 2026-04-19.
Users must track subsequent amendments themselves.
A.3.1
Recommendations
• Validate every new deployment against historical ground truth before switching traﬀic.
• Always use ExogBuilder or task_n_to_1 for feature construction. Do not hand-roll lag matrices.
• Pin n_jobs=1 (or equivalent) on the downstream regressor when bit-level reproducibility is required.
• For 𝑇> 107, process the series in windowed chunks and re-aggregate downstream.

A.5
A.5 Technical Specifications
The core task task_n_to_1 implements a deterministic sliding-window transformation.
A.5.1
Mathematical Description
Given a univariate time series 𝑋= {𝑥1, 𝑥2, … , 𝑥𝑇} and a window size 𝑤(lags), the system produces a feature
matrix 𝑋feat and target vector 𝑦via
𝑋row,𝑡= [𝑥𝑡−𝑤, 𝑥𝑡−𝑤+1, … , 𝑥𝑡−1] →𝑦𝑡= 𝑥𝑡.
A.5.2
Design Objectives
• Deterministic: Same input gives the same bit-level output.
• Leakage-free: The target 𝑦𝑡is never contained in the corresponding input vector 𝑋row,𝑡.
• Fail-safe: Invalid input raises an explicit exception; the library never silently repairs bad data.
A.5.3
Architecture (layered)
forecaster/ (low-level estimator wrappers) →preprocessing/ (deterministic transformers: ExogBuilder,
RepeatingBasisFunction, QuantileBinner, TimeSeriesDifferentiator) →model_selection/
(time-aware CV: TimeSeriesFold, OneStepAheadFold, backtesting_forecaster) →manager/ (orches-
tration: ForecasterRecursiveLGBM, ForecasterRecursiveXGB, ConfigEntsoe) →processing/ (high-
level pipelines) →tasks/ (console-script entry points).

A.7 Environmental Impact
The library itself performs no training and requires no GPU. Runtime cost is dominated by (a) NumPy/Pandas
vector ops during feature engineering and (b) whatever downstream regressor the caller passes in. A typical
ForecasterRecursiveLGBM fit on a 105-row series with 168 lags completes in seconds on a single commodity
CPU core; the per-inference carbon cost of the safe layer is effectively negligible next to the regressor’s own cost.
No pretrained weights are shipped, so there are no embedded-training emissions to report.

heitskritischen Codezeilen sind ein direkter Port aus dem skforecast-Quellcode. Ergänzender Code setzt die vier
in Kapitel 4.1 beschriebenen Code-Entwicklungsregeln um (“No dead code”, “Deterministische Transformationen”,
“Fail-safe-Verarbeitung” und “Minimaler Umfang”) sowie die vier in Kapitel 4.2 beschriebenen Prozessregeln. Durch

Softwarepakete zur Zeitreihenprognose
Das Python-Ökosystem der Zeitreihenprognose ist im vergangenen Jahrzehnt stark gewachsen und hat auch Imple-
mentationen der statitischen Programmiersprache R (R Core Team, 2021) übernommen. Grundlegend ist das Paket
statsmodels, welches ARIMA-, SARIMAX- und Exponentialglättungsmodelle in Anlehnung an die klassische Dar-
stellung von Box u. a. (2015) bereitstellt. scikit-learn (Pedregosa u. a., 2011) verzichtet bewusst auf zeitreihenspe-
zifische Funktionen und delegiert diese an nachgelagerte Bibliotheken. Die wichtigsten dieser Bibliotheken werden
kurz vorgestellt.
skforecast (Amat Rodrigo und Escobar Ortiz, 2025) stellt eine Forecaster-Abstraktion bereit, welche jeden mit
scikit-learn kompatiblen Regressor in einen rekursiven, direkten oder mehrreihigen Forecaster einhüllt. Es ist der engs-
te konzeptionelle Verwandte des hier dokumentierten Pakets. Wir übernehmen daraus die Architektur der rekursi-
ven Prognose, den Rolling-Origin-Splitter und wesentliche Teile der Module _binner, _differentiator sowie die
Residuen-Infrastruktur. Nicht übernommen werden das Visualisierungs-Subsystem (das auf matplotlib und plotly
angewiesen ist) und das Hyperparameter-Tuning mittels bayesian_search_forecaster (das auf optuna beruht und
nichtdeterministische Optimierungsspuren erzeugt). Diese Tools sind im Paket spotforecast2 enthalten.
Die vereinheitlichte Forecaster/BaseEstimator-API von sktime (Löning, A. Bagnall u. a., 2019; Löning, T. Ba-
gnall u. a., 2020), die eine Vielzahl von Modellen und Validierungsschemata bereitstellt, ist die umfangreichste aller
hier betrachteten Bibliotheken. Allerdings ist die API nicht vollständig kompatibel mit der von scikit-learn, so
dass die Integration von Regressoren aus diesem Ökosystem nicht ohne weiteres möglich ist. Zudem sind viele Model-
le in sktime auf statsmodels-Implementationen angewiesen, welche nicht für die Anforderungen der funktionalen
Sicherheit optimiert sind (z.B. keine fail-safe-Verarbeitung ungültiger Eingaben). Visualisierungstools und probabilis-
tische Backends fehlen ebenfalls.
Das Nixtla-Ökosystem, das auf eine Verbesserung des Laufzeitdurchsatzes abzielt, implementiert drei komple-
mentäre Bibliotheken: statsforecast (Garza, Challu und Mergenthaler-Canseco, 2022) stellt vektorisierte Im-
plementierungen klassischer Modelle bereit und tauscht dabei Modellflexibilität gegen aggressive Laufzeitoptimie-
rung mittels Numba (Lam, Pitrou und Seibert, 2015). mlforecast erweitert dieselbe API auf Gradient-Boosting-
Verfahren. neuralforecast bietet Deep-Learning-Architekturen über eine einheitliche Schnittstelle. Das Deep-
Learning-Backend verletzt die Regel des minimalen Umfangs unmittelbar.
Darts (Herzen u. a., 2022) führen eine vereinheitlichte API für verschiedene Zeitreihenmodelle ein. Der Installati-
onsumfang wird von optionalen Abhängigkeiten dominiert, deren Verhalten die Verfügbarkeit von Modellklassen zum
Importzeitpunkt beeinflusst. Ähnliches gilt für tsai, Merlion und Kats (Oguiza, 2023; Bhatnagar u. a., 2021; Jiang
u. a., 2022).
Keine der genannten Bibliotheken ist ingenieurtechnisch mangelhaft. Im Gegenteil, sie stellen herausragende
(Forschungs-) Software dar. Allerdings kann eine Software, die für die schnelle Exploration optimiert ist, nicht automa-
tisch ein SIL-3-Software-Verifikationsbudget erfüllen, ohne dass erhebliche betreiberspezifische Nacharbeit entsteht.
spotforecast2-safe verlagert diese Nacharbeit in das Paket selbst, so dass der Betreiber die Nachweise erbt, statt
sie reproduzieren zu müssen.

Vorverarbeitung
Das Teilpaket preprocessing enthält vier Arten von Transformatoren: Zyklische Kodierer überführen periodische
Kalendermerkmale (Stunde des Tages, Tag der Woche, Tag des Jahres) in eine glatte Darstellung. Interpolatoren re-
konstruieren kurze Lücken unter ausdrücklicher Zusicherung. Ein Quantilbinner diskretisiert ein stetiges Merkmal in
gleich häufig belegte Bins. Ein Differenzierer wendet einen Finite-Differenzen-Operator an. Alle vier Transformatoren
erben von sklearn.base.TransformerMixin und sind damit in einer Pipeline komponierbar.
3.3
Prognose
Die Prognoseschicht implementiert die rekursive Mehrschrittstrategie: Ein einzelnes skalares Ein-Schritt-voraus-
Modell wird trainiert und sodann iteriert, um Horizonte beliebiger Länge zu erzeugen (Hyndman und Athanasopoulos,
2021). Für 𝑦𝑡, Lags ℒ= {ℓ1, … , ℓ𝑝}, Fenstermerkmale 𝑤𝑡(etwa gleitende Mittel) und einen exogenen Vektor 𝑥𝑡lernt
der Forecaster
̂𝑦𝑡= 𝑓(𝑦𝑡−ℓ1, … , 𝑦𝑡−ℓ𝑝, 𝑤𝑡, 𝑥𝑡) ,
und die ℎ-Schritt-Prognose wird rekursiv gewonnen:
̂𝑦𝑡+ℎ= 𝑓( ̃𝑦𝑡+ℎ−ℓ1, … , ̃𝑦𝑡+ℎ−ℓ𝑝, 𝑤𝑡+ℎ, 𝑥𝑡+ℎ) ,
wobei ̃𝑦𝑠= 𝑦𝑠für 𝑠≤𝑡und ̃𝑦𝑠= ̂𝑦𝑠andernfalls.
Der Vorteil der rekursiven Strategien in einem sicherheitskritischen Kontext liegt darin, dass Trainings- und Aus-
wertungspfad konstruktionsbedingt gekoppelt sind: Derselbe Merkmalsmatrix-Erzeuger liefert sowohl die Trainings-
merkmale als auch die zum Vorhersagezeitpunkt verwendeten Merkmale, so dass Feature-Skew-Fehler zu einer
Übersetzungszeit- und nicht zu einer Laufzeitfehlerklasse werden. Zur Erläuterung: KI-Software verwendet zwei Pha-
sen: erst das Training mit historischen Daten, danach den Einsatz mit neuen Daten. Werden die Daten in beiden Phasen
nicht exakt gleich aufbereitet, entstehen unbemerkt Abweichungen, der sog. ”Feature-Skew”. Solche Fehler sind be-
sonders gefährlich, weil sie typischerweise erst im laufenden Betrieb auffallen, wenn bereits Schaden entstehen kann.

5.2.1
Fail-safe-NaN-Behandlung
Jeder tabellarische Messwert kann fehlen, z.B. weil eine Wetterstation eine Stunde lang keine Daten liefert, weil ein
Stromzähler neu gestartet wurde oder weil ein Importfehler eine Zelle leer gelassen hat. In Python wird eine solche
Lücke durch den Sonderwert NaN (“Not a Number”) markiert. Für die Weiterverarbeitung ist entscheidend, wie die
nachgelagerte Software auf ein solches Feld reagiert: Soll sie den leeren Wert schätzen und weiterrechnen, oder soll
sie den Vorgang anhalten und eine Entscheidung des Betreibers einfordern?
Die in der Python-Welt etablierten Zeitreihen-Bibliotheken folgen dabei überwiegend dem Muster “stillschweigend
weitermachen”. pandas (McKinney, 2010) interpoliert fehlende Werte mit Series.interpolate() linear zwischen
den Nachbarn und lässt führende wie schließende Lücken unberührt, ohne den Aufrufenden zu warnen; scikit-learn
(Pedregosa u. a., 2011) ersetzt NaN über den SimpleImputer per Vorgabe durch das Spaltenmittel; das Prognosepaket
skforecast (Amat Rodrigo und Escobar Ortiz, 2025) überträgt verbleibende NaNs in Vorhersage, wo sie sich mit
dem regulären Modellfehler vermischen; Darts (Herzen u. a., 2022) und statsmodels folgen derselben Linie. Für
exploratives Arbeiten ist diese Haltung zweckmäßig, weil sie zügiges Prototyping mit unsauberen Daten ermöglicht.
Für den Einsatz in sicherheitskritischen Umgebungen, etwa der elektrischen Lastprognose für einen Netzbetreiber, ist
sie jedoch genau der Fall, den Art. 15 KI-VO, IEC 61508 und ISO 26262 vermeiden wollen: Eine Bedienperson kann auf
der Grundlage einer scheinbar vollständigen Prognose disponieren, ohne zu bemerken, dass ein Teil der Eingangsdaten
gefehlt hat und ohne Nachfrage vom Paket ersetzt wurde.
Ein konkretes Beispiel macht den Unterschied deutlich: Angenommen, ein Netzdisponent soll für den kommenden Tag
die stündliche Last prognostizieren, und die Wetter-API liefert für eine einzelne Stunde, z.B. für 03:00 Uhr, keinen
Temperaturwert. Nach der stillschweigenden Vorgehensweise würde das Prognose-Paket den Wert linear zwischen
02:00 und 04:00 interpolieren, die Lastprognose mit scheinbar normalem Konfidenzintervall zurückliefern und der
Disponent würde die 03:00-Stunde regulär einplanen. Die Lücke in den Messwerten bliebe nur im Vorverarbeitungs-
Log erkennbar; und auch dort nur, wenn jemand sich die Mühe macht, die Log-Dateien zu lesen. Nach dem Fail-safe-
Ansatz hingegen bricht der Transformator mit einer expliziten Fehlermeldung ab, die Continuous-Integration-Pipeline
schlägt Alarm und der Betreiber muss eine zu dokumentiertende Entscheidung treffen: Er kann auf ein Fallback-Modell
umschalten, die 03:00-Stunde als ungültig markieren, oder die Lücke bewusst schließen und diese Entscheidung im
Audit-Protokoll festhalten.

from spotforecast2_safe.preprocessing import LinearlyInterpolateTS

t = LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="raise")

t = LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="ffill_bfill")
# Der Aufrufer sichert zu, NaN nachgelagert zu behandeln:
t = LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="passthrough")

SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange) ist ein standardisiertes, maschinenlesbares Format für Lizenz- und
Urheberrechts-Metadaten in Quelldateien; die Spezifikation wurde von der Linux Foundation entwickelt und 2021
als Norm ISO/IEC 5962:2021 (International Organization for Standardization und International Electrotechnical Com-
mission, 2021) ratifiziert. SPDX-Kopfzeilen wie SPDX-FileCopyrightText und SPDX-License-Identifier er-
lauben es einer Software-Stücklisten- (SBOM-) Werkzeugkette, die Lizenzlage eines Pakets ohne manuelle Sichtung
aus den Quellen zu rekonstruieren. Die REUSE Specification der Free Software Foundation Europe, aktuell in Version
3.0 (Free Software Foundation Europe, 2022), operationalisiert SPDX zu drei prüfbaren Anforderungen: (i) jede Datei
trägt im Kopf einen SPDX-FileCopyrightText- und einen SPDX-License-Identifier-Eintrag; (ii) die Volltexte
aller im Projekt verwendeten Lizenzen werden im Verzeichnis LICENSES/ abgelegt; (iii) die Einhaltung wird durch das
Werkzeug reuse lint automatisiert verifiziert. Ein Projekt ist genau dann REUSE-konform, wenn reuse lint ohne
Befund durchläuft. Die so entstehende Lizenz-Rückverfolgbarkeit adressiert die Herkunftsdokumentations-Pflichten
aus Art. 10 KI-VO (Daten-Governance) (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) und stützt die Dokumentations-
Praxis SM des IEC 62443-4-1 (Sicherheitsmanagement, Inventar von Drittanbieter-Komponenten) (IEC, 2018). Jede
Quelldatei trägt einen SPDX-Kopf. Portierte skforecast-Module tragen einen doppelten Kopf:

# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-or-later AND BSD-3-Clause

Die Normfamilie ISA/IEC 62443 ist in vier Gruppen gegliedert:
1. Allgemeines (Teil 1 — Terminologie und Modelle (IEC, 2009)),
2. Richtlinien und Verfahren (Teil 2 — Programme für Anlagenbetreiber (IEC, 2024) und Dienstleister (IEC,
2023)),
3. System (Teil 3 — Risikobewertung (IEC, 2020) und Sicherheitsanforderungen auf Systemebene (IEC, 2013))
sowie
4. Komponente (Teil 4 — sichere Produktentwicklung (IEC, 2018) und technische Anforderungen an Kompo-
nenten (IEC, 2019)).
Eine Zeitreihen-Prognosebibliothek ist in der Taxonomie der 62443-4-2 eine Software Application (neben Embedded
Device, Host Device und Network Device); sie erbt damit die Software-Application-Requirements-Teilmenge (SAR) des
Komponentenkatalogs statt des vollständigen Embedded-Device-Profils. Tabelle 14 fasst diese Gliederung zusammen.
NIST SP 800-82r3 (Stouffer u. a., 2023) stellt das Purdue-Modell, die ISA/IEC-62443-Sicht und das Industrial-Internet-
Consortium-(IIC-)Tier-Modell als drei alternative Segmentierungsframeworks nebeneinander; Abbildung 11 bildet
diese Gegenüberstellung nach. Die 62443-Darstellung verwendet dort Zones and Conduits (Enterprise →Conduit →
DMZ →Control Center →Conduit →Basic Process Control System (BPCS) →Conduit →Safety Instrumented Sys-
tem (SIS)) statt der Purdue-Ebenen 0–5. Die 62443-Reihe bildet also nicht 1:1 auf Purdue-Ebenen ab, weil ihre Teile
nach Rollen — Anlagenbetreiber, Dienstleister, Systemintegrator, Komponentenhersteller — gegliedert sind, nicht
nach Netzwerk-Ebenen. Gebräuchlich ist in der industriellen Praxis dennoch eine an den Wirkungsbereich der 62443-
Teile angelehnte Zuordnung zur Purdue-Ebene, weil sie Reviewerinnen und Prüfern die gedankliche Brücke zwischen
Netzwerksegmentierung und standardisierten Anforderungen erleichtert. Tabelle 15 fasst diese heuristische Zuordnung
zusammen; 62443-1-1 (IEC, 2009) (Terminologie und Modelle) gilt übergreifend auf allen Ebenen.

5.8.4
CPS-Besonderheiten, die den Software-Entwurf prägen
Fluchs und Rudolph (2019) und Fluchs (2024) heben vier Besonderheiten der CPS-Cybersicherheit hervor, welche sie
von klassischer IT-Sicherheit unterscheiden und die den Entwurf des vorliegenden Pakets prägen:
1. Lange Lebenszyklen. Industrielle Anlagen werden 20 bis 40 Jahre lang betrieben; ein heute ausgeliefertes
Prognosemodell kann noch im Jahr 2050 Sollwerte erzeugen. Deterministische Serialisierung, eine fixierte
öffentliche API sowie eine CPE-Kennung sind notwendige Voraussetzungen einer retrospektiven Prüfbarkeit
über diesen Horizont.
2. Konvergenz von Safety und Security. Eine Prognose, die einen physischen Aktuator steuert, ist eine sicher-
heitsfunktionale Eingabegröße. Der Technische Bericht IEC TR 63069 behandelt das gemeinsame Safety-
und-Security-Problem ausdrücklich; das Paket schließt sich dessen Schlussfolgerung an, dass Sicherheitsent-
scheidungen, einmal getroffen, nicht durch einen späteren Security-Fix überschrieben werden dürfen — daher
der fail-safe-Standardwert “Ausnahme bei ungültiger Eingabe” statt einer stillen Datenkorrektur.
3. Späte Security-Integration als dominante Fehlerursache. Interviews mit Ingenieurinnen und Ingenieuren
von INEOS und HIMA, die Fluchs (2024) berichten, zeigen, dass Security typischerweise nach der Basic-
Engineering-Phase angefügt wird, also dann, wenn die entwurfszeitlich günstigen Entscheidungen (Netzwerk-
topologie, Komponentenauswahl) bereits getroffen sind. Eine Bibliothek, die explizite Fehlerpfade und ma-
schinenlesbare Provenienz bietet, ist früh günstiger zu integrieren als eine, die Zustand verbirgt.
4. Interdisziplinäre Autorenschaft. Fluchs (2024, REQ 2.2.1) verlangen, dass Security-Entscheidungen für Nicht-
Security-Fachleute zugänglich sind. Die ausführbaren Docstrings, typisierten Verträge und dateibasierten
Audit-Protokolle des Pakets erfüllen genau diese Rolle für die Prozessingenieurin, die einen angepassten Fo-
recaster übernimmt, ohne Python- oder Security-Spezialistin zu sein.

6.1.1
Artikel 4 KI-VO (KI-Kompetenz)
Artikel 4 KI-VO (European Parliament and Council, 2024b) verpflichtet Anbieter und Betreiber, sicherzustellen, dass
ihr Personal und andere Personen, die in ihrem Auftrag ein KI-System betreiben oder verwenden, über ein hinreichendes
Maß an KI-Kompetenz verfügen, das auf den Nutzungskontext und die Personengruppen, auf die das System einwirkt,
abgestimmt ist. spotforecast2-safe ist so entworfen, dass eine Prozessingenieurin ohne formale Ausbildung im
maschinellen Lernen diese Schwelle allein durch Lektüre des Pakets selbst erreichen kann. Drei Mechanismen tragen
dazu bei. Erstens: Jeder öffentliche Transformator und jeder Forecaster führt ausführbare Docstring-Beispiele mit, so
dass das beabsichtigte Verhalten durch das Ausführen kleiner, in sich geschlossener Ausschnitte erlernt werden kann
und nicht auf das Studium externer Anleitungen angewiesen ist. Zweitens: Typisierte Verträge machen die Vor- und
Nachbedingungen jedes Aufrufs an der Aufrufstelle sichtbar; damit sinkt das Fachwissen, das zum korrekten Lesen ei-
nes Trainingsskripts erforderlich ist. Drittens: Das strukturierte Audit-Protokoll (Regel 4 in Kapitel 4) legt zeilenweise
die Abfolge der Entscheidungen offen, die ein laufender Forecaster getroffen hat, so dass das Personal des Betreibers
das betriebliche Verhalten nachträglich überprüfen kann. Die modellbezogene MODEL_CARD.md ergänzt diese Mecha-
nismen, indem sie den bestimmungsgemäßen Einsatzrahmen und die bekannten Grenzen in einer Sprache festhält,
